question: Do foundation-model parameter matrices and fine-tuning deltas behave like i.i.d. Gaussian noise, and can that hypothesis yield useful low-parameter adaptation and outlier-aware model merging methods?

key_findings.claim: Most inspected parameter histograms are roughly zero-centered and symmetric after removing values outside three standard deviations, but the analysis does not establish Gaussianity or independence.
key_findings.evidence: Across nine language, vision, and multimodal checkpoints, reported retained fractions are 99.18%-99.73%, skewness rounds to 0.00, and kurtosis ranges from 2.83 to 3.33 on the truncated values. The paper does not report Q-Q plots, distributional distances, autocorrelation/covariance tests, or comparisons to symmetric non-Gaussian alternatives; filtering the very tails also removes the region most diagnostic of Gaussianity.

key_findings.claim: The paper's inference from pooled Gaussian-looking histograms to i.i.d. coordinates is not justified, and its M-estimator argument conflates sampling variation across fitted models with the within-matrix distribution of coordinates.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 assumes coordinate independence from citations and then asserts that a pooled Gaussian histogram forces identical marginals, which does not follow. Equations 4-5 invoke asymptotic normality of an estimator around W*, but a general M-estimator has structured sandwich covariance over repeated datasets—not necessarily sigma-squared times identity—and this theorem does not say entries of one trained matrix are i.i.d. Gaussian.

anchors.section: 3.3 Revisiting the Transformation Weight Distribution, Equations 4-5

key_findings.claim: A frozen random Gaussian perturbation with one learned scalar per matrix is a surprisingly effective adaptation direction, but it remains far below full fine-tuning and does not show that task-specific deltas are noise.
key_findings.evidence: On GLUE with DeBERTaV3-base, 72 learned scalars applied to fixed Gaussian matrices average 78.62 versus 71.69 for head-only, 73.87 for SVDiff, and 88.24 for full fine-tuning. Five random runs are averaged. A useful random high-dimensional direction plus learned layer scales is compatible with overparameterization and does not imply equivalence between learned transformations and i.i.d. noise.

key_findings.claim: Adding a learned global weight-scaling/Gaussian component to LoRA improves the reported commonsense benchmark averages, although the study does not compare against equally tuned modern PEFT alternatives or provide uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: For ranks 16 and 32 on LLaMA-7B, LLaMA2-7B, and LLaMA3-8B, the augmentation improves the eight-task average by 0.9 to 7.8 points at the same listed trainable-parameter percentage. The construction W'=(s+1)W+AB is effectively a learned scale on each pretrained weight matrix plus LoRA when W initializes the perturbation.

anchors.section: 5.1 Parameter Efficient Fine-tuning, Equation 6 and Table 3

key_findings.claim: Outlier-preserving averaging beats naive averaging for one two-expert multimodal merge, but the evidence is too narrow to establish a general model-merging advantage.
key_findings.evidence: Merging instruction-tuned LLaVA-1.6-13B and Math-LLaVA, preserving task-delta entries beyond 2 sigma and averaging the rest raises the seven-benchmark average from 42.5 to 44.5. No TIES, task-arithmetic, low-rank, sign-conflict, or learned-merging baseline is evaluated, and only one pair of closely related experts is tested.

method.core_idea: Characterize elementwise histograms of pretrained and fine-tuning weight matrices, hypothesize an optimal sparse signal hidden by additive Gaussian training noise, and turn the hypothesis into learned per-matrix perturbation scales and magnitude-thresholded merging.
method.mechanism: The analysis truncates each matrix to mean plus or minus three standard deviations and summarizes skewness/kurtosis. Adaptation freezes a sampled Gaussian matrix or the pretrained matrix and learns scalar amplitudes, optionally alongside LoRA. Merging classifies task-vector entries beyond a multiple of the minimum per-group standard deviation as outliers, preserves them, and averages the remaining entries.
assumptions: Element histograms pooled within a matrix are informative about joint coordinate structure.
Asymptotic M-estimator normality applies to deep-network weights with an isotropic covariance and can be interpreted coordinatewise within a single model.
Magnitude relative to a matrix-wide standard deviation reliably separates task signal from Gaussian noise.
The optimal parameter vector is sparse, symmetric, zero-mean, truncated-Gaussian, and contains a few outliers.
Benchmark gains from scalar random perturbations validate the proposed distributional mechanism rather than a more generic weight-rescaling or random-subspace effect.

techniques.role: Summarizes central weight histograms using retained ratio, skewness, and kurtosis after 3-sigma filtering.
Adapts each frozen weight matrix along a fixed random Gaussian direction using one learned scalar.
Adds per-matrix scaling of the base weights to the usual low-rank update.
Keeps large task-vector entries separate while averaging presumed Gaussian central entries.
Illustrates how a hypothesized sparse truncated-Gaussian signal could be obscured by increasing Gaussian perturbations.

evaluations.setting: Layer/module parameter histograms from nine NLP, vision, and multimodal foundation checkpoints plus LoRA-Dash/DoRA transformation weights.
evaluations.metric: Three-sigma retained fraction, skewness, kurtosis, and visual histogram shape.
evaluations.result: Central histograms are near symmetric and mesokurtic on average, with some sharp, inverted-T, or near-linear exceptions.
evaluations.baseline: Theoretical skewness 0 and non-Fisher kurtosis 3 of a Gaussian.

evaluations.setting: DeBERTaV3-base GLUE adaptation using 72 learned scalar amplitudes over fixed Gaussian delta matrices, averaged over five runs.
evaluations.metric: Mean of eight development-set task metrics and trainable parameter count.
evaluations.result: 78.62 average with 72 scalars, above head-only 71.69 and SVDiff 73.87, but below full fine-tuning 88.24.
evaluations.baseline: Head-only tuning, full fine-tuning, and SVDiff.

evaluations.setting: Rank-16/32 LoRA on LLaMA-7B, LLaMA2-7B, and LLaMA3-8B over eight commonsense tasks, with or without pretrained-weight scaling.
evaluations.result: The proposed augmentation improves all six listed configurations by 0.9-7.8 points.

evaluations.setting: Merge of one instruction and one math LLaVA-13B expert over seven vision-language benchmarks.
evaluations.result: Sigma-2 outlier preservation reaches 44.5 versus naive averaging's 42.5.
evaluations.baseline: Plain weight averaging; no strong contemporary merging baselines.

limitations: Gaussianity is assessed after tail truncation using only two low-order moments; this cannot distinguish many symmetric distributions and biases the tail conclusion.
No empirical independence test is performed, and pooled element histograms cannot reveal correlations, low-rank structure, row/column heterogeneity, or spectral organization.
The asymptotic-normality argument is applied with an unjustified isotropic covariance and to the wrong sampling object.
The hypothesized optimal sparse truncated-Gaussian W* is illustrated synthetically rather than identified from trained models.
PEFT comparisons omit modern random-subspace, scaling, and Gaussian-noise alternatives, and uncertainty/significance reporting is limited.
Model merging is evaluated on only two related experts with naive averaging as the sole baseline.
Elementwise distribution is not invariant to reparameterization, channel permutations, normalization folding, or matrix rescaling, limiting claims of intrinsic weight mechanisms.
failure_modes: A non-Gaussian symmetric central distribution passes skewness/kurtosis checks after its informative tails are removed.
Strong row, column, or spectral correlations coexist with a Gaussian-looking marginal histogram, invalidating an i.i.d. interpretation.
Large-magnitude entries reflect scale conventions or normalization rather than semantic task outliers.
Random perturbation gains disappear under stronger weight-scaling, intrinsic-dimension, or PEFT baselines.
Outlier-preserving merge accumulates conflicting large entries as the number or diversity of experts grows.
reusable_insights: Weight-distribution studies should combine marginals with correlation, spectral, reparameterization, and functional perturbation tests.
A learned scalar per matrix is a useful ultra-low-parameter baseline for PEFT because it tests whether simple layerwise rescaling explains purported structure.
Claims about Gaussianity should be tested on held-out tails and against matched-moment alternatives, not inferred from skewness and kurtosis alone.
Outlier-aware merging needs sign-conflict and multi-expert stress tests before magnitude can be treated as importance.
Exact distinctions among randomness over training runs, posterior uncertainty, and within-tensor coordinate distributions are essential in statistical arguments about weights.
open_questions: How much of the reported PEFT gain is reproduced by deterministic per-matrix scaling, random orthogonal directions, or intrinsic-subspace tuning?
Do weight entries remain approximately Gaussian under rigorous goodness-of-fit tests without truncation and after conditioning on row, column, head, and layer roles?
Which functionally invariant statistics—spectra, activation covariances, or Fisher geometry—best predict adaptation and merge success?
Can outlier thresholds be learned or calibrated using conflict and curvature rather than a global standard deviation?
Does the proposed merging rule remain competitive for many experts, heterogeneous architectures, and non-local merges?

competitive_landscape.title: Bayesian Neural Network Priors Revisited
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct empirical counterpoint studying summary statistics of weights learned by SGD to design realistic priors.
competitive_landscape.difference: Fortuin et al. report strong spatial correlations in convolutional weights and heavy-tailed fully connected weights, explicitly rejecting a simple independent isotropic Gaussian description; the target relies mainly on pooled central histograms.

competitive_landscape.title: Traditional and Heavy Tailed Self Regularization in Neural Network Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Established weight-matrix analysis that uses empirical spectral densities to expose trained correlations and heavy-tailed structure invisible to entry histograms.
competitive_landscape.difference: Mahoney and Martin characterize matrix-level spectral universality and its relation to training/generalization; the target asserts coordinatewise Gaussian noise from marginal moments.

competitive_landscape.title: GIFT-SW: Gaussian noise Injected Fine-Tuning of Salient Weights for LLMs
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior practical competitor combining Gaussian perturbations with parameter-efficient fine-tuning of salient LLM weights.
competitive_landscape.difference: GIFT-SW selects sensitive columns and injects noise into nonsalient ones under a compute budget; the target learns scalar amplitudes for whole random matrices and ties this to a global Gaussian-weight hypothesis.

competitive_landscape.title: TIES-Merging: Resolving Interference When Merging Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Strong direct model-merging baseline that also trims small deltas but explicitly resolves sign conflicts.
competitive_landscape.difference: TIES validates across modalities, architectures, task counts, and sizes; the target uses a sigma magnitude split without sign election and tests one two-model merge.

competitive_landscape.title: BERT Busters: Outlier Dimensions that Disrupt Transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Functional study showing that a tiny set of structured high-magnitude Transformer parameters can be causally important.
competitive_landscape.difference: Kovaleva et al. locate recurring LayerNorm dimensions and ablate them to establish causal importance; the target classifies outliers by global magnitude and infers their role from merging performance.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference after checking trained-weight priors, spectral heavy-tail work, Gaussian-noise PEFT, outlier studies, and TIES merging: the paper's useful novelty is the extremely small scalar-over-random-matrix adaptation baseline and the simple sigma-thresholded LLaVA merge. Its broad claims that LFM weights are i.i.d. Gaussian noise and that optimal weights have a specific sparse truncated-Gaussian form are not supported by the reported tests and conflict with matrix-level correlation/heavy-tail evidence. The applications merit controlled follow-up independently of the proposed statistical mechanism.
reviewer_notes: Read all 41 extracted pages, including full per-layer histograms, synthetic W-star construction, standard-deviation analyses, algorithms, and experiment details. The review distinguishes observed central marginal shape from the paper's much stronger independence, isotropy, and optimal-weight claims. Competitor records were checked on primary OpenReview, PMLR, and arXiv pages on 2026-08-23.
